name: Martin Gardner
knownFor: The writer who made recreational mathematics popular, through his "Mathematical Games" column.
bio: Martin Gardner was born in Tulsa and studied philosophy at the University of Chicago, graduating in 1936. He never took a mathematics course after high school; he came to the subject as a writer, editor and amateur magician, and that is part of why he explained it so well.

In 1956 a free-standing article on hexaflexagons in Scientific American led to a regular column, "Mathematical Games", which ran for twenty-five years and brought puzzles, paradoxes and new mathematics to a general audience. He published more than a hundred books, and was also a leading sceptic of pseudoscience and a leading authority on Lewis Carroll.

events.text: Took his bachelor's degree in philosophy at the University of Chicago.
Published his first book, In the Name of Science, an enlargement of a 1950 Antioch Review article.
A hexaflexagon article in the December issue of Scientific American began the "Mathematical Games" column.
Fads and Fallacies in the Name of Science was published.
Joined fellow sceptics to found CSICOP, an organisation for testing extraordinary claims.
The June issue carried the last instalment of the column under its original title.

relevance: Gardner is the doyen of American puzzlers. His column made recreational mathematics a mainstream interest for the second half of the twentieth century, and his annotated Alice is the standard way into Lewis Carroll's logic and wordplay.
influence: His admirers included W. H. Auden, Arthur C. Clarke, Carl Sagan, Isaac Asimov and Richard Dawkins, and a whole community of puzzle-makers meets every two years in his memory.
